name: Chemical Structure & Reactivity
tagline: Electronic effects, steric factors, and structure-reactivity relationships.

definition.lead: This field connects a molecule's structure to the way it reacts: where the electrons sit decides where, how fast and how selectively bonds break and form.
definition.body: Electronic effects, steric bulk and orbital overlap explain why one carbon reacts and its neighbour doesn't. Mastering these patterns lets chemists predict products instead of memorizing them.

timeline.title: Shared electron pairs
timeline.text: Gilbert N. Lewis describes the covalent bond as a shared pair of electrons.

timeline.title: Curly arrows
timeline.text: William Kermack and Robert Robinson draw electron movement with curved arrows.
timeline.why: The notation every chemist now uses.

timeline.title: New acids and bases
timeline.text: Brønsted and Lowry define acids as proton donors; Lewis as electron-pair acceptors.
timeline.why: Unified a huge range of reactions.

timeline.title: SN1 and SN2
timeline.text: Edward Hughes and Christopher Ingold classify substitution mechanisms.
timeline.why: Kinetics revealed how bonds break and form.

timeline.title: The Hammett equation
timeline.text: Louis Hammett relates substituents to rates and equilibria.

timeline.title: Frontier orbitals
timeline.text: Kenichi Fukui shows that the HOMO and LUMO control reactivity.
timeline.why: A simple orbital picture for predicting reactions.

timeline.title: The Hammond postulate
timeline.text: George Hammond links the structure of a transition state to its energy.
timeline.why: A rule of thumb used in every mechanism discussion.

timeline.title: Hard and soft acids and bases
timeline.text: Ralph Pearson introduces the HSAB principle.
timeline.why: Predicts which partners prefer each other.

timeline.title: Orbital symmetry
timeline.text: Robert Woodward and Roald Hoffmann publish their rules for pericyclic reactions.
timeline.why: Explained reactions once thought to have no mechanism.

timeline.title: A Nobel for reactivity theory
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Kenichi Fukui and Roald Hoffmann.
timeline.why: Theory became a working tool for synthetic chemists.

quiz.explain: The phenoxide anion spreads its charge into the aromatic ring by resonance.

quiz.q: An electron-withdrawing group on benzoic acid makes the acid…
quiz.explain: Pulling electron density stabilizes the carboxylate anion.

quiz.q: Why does tert-butyl bromide not react by SN2?
options: Three methyl groups block back-side attack
quiz.explain: It reacts by SN1 instead, through a stable tertiary carbocation.

quiz.q: In HSAB theory, soft acids prefer…
quiz.explain: Large, polarizable partners pair up, as do small, highly charged ones.

quiz.q: By the Hammond postulate, the transition state of a strongly exothermic step resembles…
quiz.explain: It comes early on the path, close in energy to the reactants.
BF₃ and AlCl₃ are classic examples.

quiz.q: What is the order of carbocation stability?
quiz.explain: Alkyl groups donate electron density and stabilize the positive charge.

quiz.q: In a carbonyl group, which atom is attacked by nucleophiles?
quiz.explain: Oxygen pulls electrons away, leaving the carbon partially positive.

quiz.q: A positive Hammett ρ value means the reaction is…
quiz.explain: Negative charge builds up in the transition state, and withdrawing groups stabilize it.

quiz.q: Who classified substitution mechanisms as SN1 and SN2 in 1935?
quiz.explain: They used kinetics and stereochemistry to tell the two apart.

quiz.q: A curly arrow in a mechanism shows the movement of…
quiz.explain: A half-headed (fish-hook) arrow shows a single electron.
